title: Cold Oak Shelter, Lee County
summary: At Cold Oak, a rock overhang in Lee County, Late Archaic families of about 1200–1000 BC stored seeds of sunflower, goosefoot, and squash they had grown themselves.
bodyMarkdown:
Three thousand years ago, families came back again and again to a dry rock overhang in what is now Lee County. In its shelter they cracked nuts, worked wood, twisted cordage, and dug storage pits. What they put in those pits has made Cold Oak one of the places archaeologists turn to when they ask how farming began in eastern North America.

## Who lived here, and when

The main use of the shelter [dates to the end of the Late Archaic period](https://archaeology.ky.gov/Find-a-Site/Pages/Cold-Oak.aspx), about 1200 to 1000 BC. People did not live there year-round in one long stay. The plant remains and tools show they used it seasonally, returning through the different parts of the year. These were still hunter-gatherers, and they still leaned on what the woods gave them.

But by about 1200 BC they were also relying more and more on crops from their own gardens.

## What the pits held

The dry deposits preserved things that usually rot away. Wild foods were mostly hickory nuts, walnuts, red and white oak acorns, and chestnuts. In the storage pits were charred and uncharred seeds of sunflower, goosefoot, knotweed, marshelder, and squash, and possibly maygrass. Every one of these belongs to the [Eastern Agricultural Complex](https://grokipedia.com/page/Eastern_Agricultural_Complex), the suite of native plants that makes eastern North America one of roughly ten places in the world where people independently domesticated crops.

Many of those plants look like weeds today. Goosefoot and knotweed grow in any disturbed ground. But they yield heavy crops of small starchy seeds, while sunflower and marshelder give oily ones. Archaeologists recognize domestication in them through slow changes over centuries: bigger seeds, different shapes, and thinner seed coats that sprout readily when planted.

Other finds fill in daily life. Bits of cordage and a wooden tool that may have been used in weaving point to textile work. Piles of wood chips and part of a stone celt suggest woodworking. Hunters brought back white-tailed deer, turkey, squirrel, and black bear, and the shelter also held box turtle, fish bone, crayfish, and freshwater mussel shell.

## Why grow seeds?

Archaeologists still argue about why foragers began to plant. Some think garden seeds made up for nut harvests that failed in some years. Others see stored seed as a buffer for the lean months of late winter. Kristen Gremillion’s [1993 study of plant husbandry at Cold Oak](https://core.tdar.org/document/171329/plant-husbandry-at-the-archaic-woodland-transition-evidence-from-the-coal-oak-shelter-kentucky) placed the site at the Archaic–Woodland transition.

Her [later work on preserved human paleofeces](https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/american-antiquity/article/abs/early-agricultural-diet-in-eastern-north-america-evidence-from-two-kentucky-rockshelters/88B3E53127B049BBA16EE784ACCF7CF5) from two eastern Kentucky rockshelters found that native crops were sometimes a real part of the diet by about 1000 BC, a thousand years before farming economies spread across the region.

## Kentucky today

Forest Service archaeologists recorded the site in 1983 and dug there in 1984, and an Ohio State University team returned in 1994. Those are study dates; the story and its pin use the years people lived there.

Cold Oak is a protected archaeological site. This story names the county but does not map the shelter, and the pin is a rounded, county-level point. Digging or collecting at archaeological sites without permission is a crime in Kentucky.
